title: TypeScript
blurb: Structural typing, narrowing, generics, and the boundary where types stop being guarantees. Nearly every JS role now screens on this.

questions.q: What is the difference between `any` and `unknown`?
choices: `unknown` switches off checking; `any` accepts anything but must be narrowed first
`any` is erased at compile time, while `unknown` survives as a runtime type check
`any` switches off checking; `unknown` accepts anything but must be narrowed first
They behave the same; `unknown` is simply the name that newer lint rules prefer
questions.why: `any` is contagious: everything derived from it is unchecked too. `unknown` is the safe top type: you can assign anything to it, but you cannot call, index or read it until you narrow it. Neither survives compilation, so the 'runtime check' option is wrong.
questions.asked: The clearest signal of whether someone uses TypeScript or just tolerates it.

questions.q: Does TypeScript check types at runtime?
choices: No: types are erased at compile time, so nothing is checked when the code runs
Partly: interfaces are erased, but type aliases are kept for `instanceof` checks
Yes: the emitted JavaScript keeps type checks at every function boundary
Only in development builds, where the bundler injects runtime assertions
questions.why: Type annotations are stripped from the output. That is why `typeof` and `instanceof` are the runtime tools, why you cannot `switch` on a type, and why data crossing the network needs real validation rather than an annotation.
questions.asked: It sets up the follow-up that matters: how do you validate an API response, then?

questions.q: What is wrong with this line?
questions.code: const user = await (await fetch('/api/me')).json() as User;
choices: `as` cannot be applied to an awaited expression, so this fails to compile
Nothing: `json()` is generic, so `as User` just fills in its type argument
Nothing: `fetch` rejects a body that does not match the declared type
`as` asserts without checking, so a changed API shape goes unnoticed
questions.why: `json()` returns `Promise<any>`; `as User` tells the compiler to stop asking and nothing verifies the shape. `fetch` knows nothing about your types. Validate at the boundary with a schema library or a hand-written type guard.
questions.asked: The single most valuable TypeScript question for a CRUD role: it separates typed code from checked data.

questions.q: What is the type of `config.port` here?
questions.code:
type Config = { mode: 'dark' | 'light'; port: string | number };
const config = { mode: 'dark', port: 8080 } satisfies Config;
choices: `string | number`, because `satisfies` applies the declared type
`number`, because `satisfies` checks but keeps the inferred type
`any`, because `satisfies` only runs its check at runtime
`8080`, because `satisfies` makes every property a literal
questions.why: `satisfies` errors if the object does not fit `Config`, but the variable keeps its own inferred type, so `config.port` is `number` and `toFixed` works without narrowing. An annotation (`const config: Config`) would widen it to `string | number`; `as` would not check it at all.
questions.asked: A newer operator, so it signals whether someone keeps current, and it tests the annotation-versus-inference distinction.

questions.q: What is a discriminated union?
choices: A union of primitive types that the compiler sorts from widest to narrowest
A union of object types sharing a literal tag field the compiler narrows on
A union with `null` and `undefined` removed by the `NonNullable` helper
An interface whose optional fields are checked by a runtime discriminator
questions.why: `{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'error'; error: Error } | { status: 'ok'; data: T }`. Checking `state.status === 'ok'` narrows the whole object, so `state.data` exists only where it can. Optional fields cannot give you that guarantee.
questions.asked: Describe this well and you have effectively answered 'how do you model loading states?' too.

questions.q: How do you make a `switch` over a union exhaustive, so a new member breaks the build?
choices: Add `default: break` so any unhandled member falls through quietly
Enable `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, which checks every union member
Replace the `switch` with `if`/`else`, which the compiler checks fully
Assign the value to a `never` variable in the `default` branch
questions.why: `default: { const _exhaustive: never = value; throw new Error(...) }`. When someone adds a union member, that assignment stops compiling at every switch that forgot it. `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` only stops cases running into each other; it says nothing about missing members.
questions.asked: It shows you use the type system as a refactoring safety net, which is the real pitch for TypeScript.

questions.q: Is TypeScript structurally or nominally typed?
choices: Structurally: compatibility is decided by shape, not by the declared name
Nominally: two types are related only if one is declared to extend the other
Nominally, unless a class opts in to structural checks with `implements`
It depends on the tsconfig: `strict` switches the checker to nominal typing
questions.why: Any object with the right properties satisfies an interface, even if it never declared it. That is why a `UserId` and an `OrderId` that are both `string` are interchangeable, and why branded types exist. The exception: a class with `private`, `protected` or `#` members is compatible only with its own lineage.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually 'so how would you stop two string ids being swapped?', which leads to branded types.

questions.q: What is a branded type and why use one?
choices: A type imported from a specific npm package, so its origin is tracked
A type alias exported from its own module so it cannot be recreated
A primitive intersected with a unique marker, so distinct ids cannot be swapped
A type alias with a JSDoc tag that the compiler enforces on each call site
questions.why: `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }`. Passing an `OrderId` where a `UserId` is expected now fails to compile, though both are strings at runtime. A type alias from its own module is still just `string` structurally. It costs one cast where ids are created.
questions.asked: It comes up as 'how would you stop someone passing the wrong id?', a real bug class in CRUD code.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `interface` and `type`?
choices: Interfaces are for classes and emit a runtime object; type aliases are erased
Type aliases merge when re-declared; only interfaces can express unions and tuples
Type aliases are the legacy form and are deprecated in favour of interfaces
Interfaces merge when re-declared; only type aliases can express unions and tuples
questions.why: Declaration merging matters when augmenting a library's types. Type aliases are the only way to write a union, a conditional type or a template literal type. Neither emits runtime code. For a plain object shape, either works: pick one and be consistent.
questions.asked: A guaranteed question. The weak answer is 'interfaces are for classes'.

questions.q: What does `strictNullChecks` change?
choices: `null` becomes a compile error anywhere, so optional values must use `undefined`
The compiler inserts runtime null checks before every property access it emits
`null` and `undefined` stop being assignable to every type, so absence is explicit
Only function parameters are checked for null; locals and fields stay unchecked
questions.why: Without it, `string` silently includes `null`, so the compiler cannot warn you. With it you write `string | null` where absence is real, and the compiler forces a check before use. It emits no runtime code; it is the highest-value flag in the config.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know what `strict` actually buys you, rather than treating it as a magic switch.

questions.q: What is the difference between `foo?: string` and `foo: string | undefined`?
choices: The optional form also accepts `null`; the union form accepts only `undefined`
The union form must be present, possibly `undefined`; the optional one may be omitted
They are identical, and the compiler rewrites one into the other when it checks
The optional form must be present but may be `undefined`; the union may be omitted
questions.why: `?:` means the key may be absent; the union means the key is required but its value may be `undefined`. In a PATCH, 'key absent' means leave alone, and on the wire 'clear it' must be `null` because JSON drops `undefined`. The distinction matters in-process, and sharpens under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.
questions.asked: A precise question that maps onto a real API design decision: how a PATCH says 'leave alone' versus 'clear'.

questions.q: What does `B` resolve to?
questions.code:
type A = { id: number; name: string };
type B = Omit<A, 'name'> & { name: number };
choices: { id: number; name: number }
{ id: number; name: string & number }
{ id: number; name: string | number }
{ id: number }
questions.why: `Omit` removes `name` first, so the intersection adds it back with the new type. Without the `Omit`, `name` would be `string & number`, which is `never`. This is the standard idiom for overriding one field of an existing type.
questions.asked: It is the idiom behind most DTO types, so it shows whether you can read everyday type code.

questions.q: What does `Partial<T>` do?
choices: Makes every property of `T` readonly
Removes `undefined` from each property of `T`
Makes every property of `T` optional
Makes every nested property of `T` optional
questions.why: It is useful for a PATCH payload or an options object; its counterpart is `Required<T>`. It is shallow: nested objects keep their required fields, so it is not a deep partial.
questions.asked: A warm-up that often leads into 'how would you type a PATCH body?'.

questions.q: When is a generic type parameter actually needed?
choices: When the input and output types must stay related to each other
Whenever a function accepts an object argument of any kind
Always, as the type-safe way to avoid writing `any` in a signature
Only in published library code, never in application code
questions.why: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` carries the element type through. A type parameter used once and related to nothing else adds no safety over `unknown`; it is `any` with extra syntax.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check whether generics are understood or cargo-culted.

questions.q: What does `Keys` resolve to?
questions.code: type Keys = keyof { id: number; name: string };
choices: string
['id', 'name']
number | string
'id' | 'name'
questions.why: `keyof` gives a union of the literal key types, not a tuple and not the value types. Combined with a constraint it gives a type-safe getter: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`.
questions.asked: The `get` function built on it is one of the most common TypeScript live-coding exercises.

questions.q: Why does this fail to compile?
choices: The callback parameter `s` needs an explicit `string` annotation
`map` does not exist on `string`, so the union must be narrowed
A union of a type and its own array type is not allowed
`trim` is not available on the elements of a union array
questions.why: On a union you can only use members present on every branch, and `string` has no `map`. Narrow with `Array.isArray(input)` first, or normalise the input to an array at the top of the function.
questions.asked: It checks that you read compiler errors on unions as 'narrow first', not as 'add a cast'.

questions.q: What is a user-defined type guard?
choices: A decorator that validates a parameter before the method body runs
A function returning `arg is Type`, which narrows the argument for the caller
A compiler flag that inserts `typeof` checks at every function boundary
A cast written as `<Type>arg`, the older syntax for an `as` assertion
questions.why: `function isUser(v: unknown): v is User { ... }`. The compiler trusts the signature, so the body has to really check; a lazy guard is an `as` with more steps.
questions.asked: The follow-up is 'what happens if the guard's body is wrong?', which tests whether you know the compiler trusts it blindly.

questions.q: Given `const cfg: { readonly port: number } = load()`, what does `readonly` stop?
choices: Any change to `port` at runtime, because the object is frozen on creation
Reads of `port` outside the module that declared the type
Assignment to `port` and to every nested property below it
Assignment to `port` through `cfg`, at compile time only
questions.why: Types are erased, so `readonly` only stops writes through that type during compilation; another alias without `readonly` can still mutate the object. It is also shallow. `Object.freeze` is the runtime tool, and it is shallow too.
questions.asked: It separates people who know types are erased from people who think the compiler protects the running program.

questions.q: What type does `routes` get?
questions.code: const routes = ['home', 'about'] as const;
choices: readonly ['home', 'about']
string[], with the array frozen at runtime
('home' | 'about')[]
readonly string[]
questions.why: `as const` infers the narrowest literal types and makes the result readonly, so this is a readonly tuple of literals. It does nothing at runtime. With it you can derive a union: `type Route = typeof routes[number]`, which is `'home' | 'about'`.
questions.asked: A very practical trick: one source of truth for both a runtime list and a type.

questions.q: For a status field sent to and from a JSON API, why do many teams prefer a string-literal union over an `enum`?
choices: An enum is not type-safe, because any string can be assigned to one
A union is faster at runtime, because enum lookups go through an object
A union erases completely and matches the JSON values you actually send
An enum cannot be used in a `switch`, so exhaustiveness checks fail
questions.why: A union of `'draft' | 'published'` emits no code and is exactly the JSON on the wire. A regular enum emits a runtime object, string enums reject the raw string from JSON without a cast, and numeric enums serialise as numbers. Enums do work in `switch`; that option is simply false.
questions.asked: An 'explain your preference' question: either choice is defensible if you can name the trade-off.

questions.q: What is the type of `config.mode`?
questions.code: const config = { retries: 3, mode: 'dark' };
choices: 'dark'
any
readonly 'dark'
string
questions.why: Properties of an object literal are mutable, so they widen to their base type: you could assign `config.mode = 'light'` later. `as const`, or a contextual type with a literal union, keeps the literal.
questions.asked: It explains the common 'Type string is not assignable to type "dark" | "light"' error that juniors hit daily.

questions.q: What is the `Result` pattern and why use it instead of throwing?
choices: A helper that retries a failing call and returns its final outcome
A wrapper that converts any thrown exception into a `null` return value
Returning `{ ok, value } | { ok, error }` so failure appears in the type
A replacement for every try/catch, including for programming errors
questions.why: A thrown error is invisible to the type system; nothing forces a caller to handle it. A Result puts the failure path in the signature. It is verbose, so most codebases use it for expected failures and still throw for bugs, which is why 'replace every try/catch' is wrong.
questions.asked: A design-opinion question that maps onto the same exceptions-versus-Result debate in C#.

questions.q: What does the `!` do here?
questions.code: const el = document.getElementById('root')!;
choices: It throws a descriptive error at runtime if the element is missing
It removes `null` from the type, with no check when the code runs
It converts a `null` result into `undefined` for optional chaining
It waits for the element to exist before returning it to the caller
questions.why: It is `as NonNullable<T>` in one character and emits nothing. Fine where you genuinely know more than the compiler, but `if (!el) throw new Error('#root is missing')` gives a real error message instead of a later 'cannot read properties of null'.
questions.asked: Reviewers flag `!` constantly; knowing when it is a lie is the point.

questions.q: What does `Record<'draft' | 'live', number>` require?
choices: An object with both `draft` and `live` keys, each holding a number
An array of two numbers indexed by the strings `'draft'` and `'live'`
An object with a `draft` or a `live` key, whose value is a number
An object with any string keys, as long as every value is a number
questions.why: With a union of literal keys, `Record` requires every key, so a lookup table fails to compile when the union grows and nobody adds the new entry. `Record<string, number>` is the open-ended dictionary form.
questions.asked: It leads into using the compiler to keep lookup tables complete as a union grows.

questions.q: Why can this crash at runtime although it compiles under `strict`?
choices: `strict` turns index reads into `any`, so `user` is no longer checked
`Record` is erased, so `map[id]` returns the whole object at runtime
Indexing is typed `User` even when the key is missing from the object
`id` might be a number, and numeric keys are not stored in a Record
questions.why: By default TypeScript assumes any index into a record or array succeeds. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (not part of `strict`) adds `| undefined` to every index access and forces a check: noisier, but it catches real crashes.
questions.asked: A strong signal: it shows you have tuned a tsconfig rather than accepted the defaults.

questions.q: What is the type of `x` at each `return`?
choices: string at the first, number at the second
string | number at both returns
string at the first, string | number at the second
string at the first, unknown at the second
questions.why: Control-flow analysis narrows inside the branch and also narrows the rest of the function by elimination, because the string case has already returned. That is why an early return is often the cleanest way to narrow.
questions.asked: It checks that you know narrowing continues after an early return, which shapes how you write guards.

questions.q: What is the `never` type used for?
choices: Marking APIs as deprecated so the editor strikes through each call site
Typing a function that returns nothing, as another spelling of `void`
Typing a value that is always `null`, such as a cleared field
Exhaustiveness checks, and functions that always throw or never return
questions.why: `never` has no values: nothing is assignable to it, which is what makes the exhaustive-switch trick work. A function that always throws is inferred as returning `never`. `void` is different: the function returns, just with nothing useful.
questions.asked: It checks you can explain the exhaustive-switch trick rather than copy it.

questions.q: Why does `items.forEach(x => set.add(x))` type-check, when `set.add` returns the Set?
choices: `forEach` is typed with `any` for the callback's return value
A callback typed `() => void` may return anything; it is ignored
Arrow functions with one expression are always inferred as `void`
The compiler inserts a `return undefined` into inline callbacks
questions.why: Assigning a function to a `void`-returning function type deliberately allows any return value, because the caller promises to ignore it. A callback type returning `undefined` would reject `set.add`. The arrow itself still infers `Set<number>`; nothing is rewritten.
questions.asked: An edge case that explains why `void` and `undefined` are not interchangeable as return types.

questions.q: Which signature types a getter that returns the property's own type?
choices: `function get(obj: object, key: string): any`
`function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`
`function get<T>(obj: T, key: string): T`
`function get(obj: Record<string, unknown>, key: string): unknown`
questions.why: The constraint ties the key to the object and the indexed access type ties the return to the key, so `get(user, 'name')` is `string` and `get(user, 'nope')` fails to compile. The `unknown` version is safe but forces a cast at every call.
questions.asked: The canonical 'write me a generic' exercise.

questions.q: What does `Pick<T, K>` do, and what is its opposite?
choices: It makes keys `K` optional; `Required<T, K>` reverses it
It extracts union members `K`; `Exclude<T, K>` drops them
It keeps the first `K` keys; `Drop<T, K>` removes them
It keeps only keys `K`; `Omit<T, K>` removes them instead
questions.why: Both derive a DTO from a domain model, e.g. `type PublicUser = Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>`. `Extract`/`Exclude` work on union members, not object keys. Note that with `Omit`, a sensitive field added later is included by default; `Pick` is the safer allow-list.
questions.asked: It usually leads to 'which is safer for a public DTO?', where Pick's allow-list wins.

questions.q: Under `strict`, what happens with this code?
choices: It compiles, and a non-Dog ends up inside `dogs`
A compile error on the assignment `animals = dogs`
A compile error on the `push`, which lacks `breed`
It compiles, then `push` throws a runtime TypeError
questions.why: Arrays are covariant in TypeScript for ergonomics, so `Dog[]` is assignable to `Animal[]`, and pushing an `Animal` through that alias is allowed. The result is unsound: `dogs` now holds an object with no `breed`, and nothing throws. Type a parameter you only read from as `readonly Animal[]`, which has no `push`.
questions.asked: A deep-end question: knowing the hole exists is worth more than being able to name 'covariance'.

questions.q: What is the safest way to type a JSON payload whose shape you do not control?
choices: Type it as `any` and read fields directly, since JSON has no methods
Cast it with `as` to the interface the API documentation describes
Type it as `unknown`, then validate it with a schema or a type guard
Wrap every property access in try/catch so a bad shape cannot crash
questions.why: Validation is the only thing that turns runtime data into a type you can trust. Libraries like Zod derive the static type from the runtime schema, so the two cannot drift. A cast trusts the documentation, which is exactly what goes stale.
questions.asked: The practical heart of TypeScript in a CRUD app.

questions.q: What does 'make impossible states unrepresentable' mean?
choices: Throwing early whenever a function receives a combination of invalid inputs
Marking every field `readonly` so no code can put an object in a bad state
Validating every form in the UI layer so bad states never reach the server
Modelling types so that contradictory combinations cannot be constructed
questions.why: `{ loading: boolean; data?: T; error?: Error }` permits loading, errored and loaded at once. A discriminated union permits exactly three states, so half the defensive code disappears. Throwing and validating handle bad states at runtime; this prevents them at compile time.
questions.asked: Using the phrase correctly signals real type-design experience.

questions.q: What does a `.d.ts` file contain?
choices: The compiled JavaScript output, minified for publishing to npm
Default compiler options that a tsconfig can inherit from
Type declarations only, describing code that exists elsewhere
Documentation comments extracted for the editor's hover text
questions.why: Declaration files hold ambient types with no runtime code. They are how `@types/*` packages describe untyped libraries, and how you declare globals or module augmentations in your own project. Shared compiler options live in a base tsconfig reached through `extends`.
questions.asked: It comes up when a library has no types, and the follow-up is 'what would you do about it?'.

questions.q: What does `Handler` resolve to?
questions.code: type Handler = `on${Capitalize<'click' | 'focus'>}`;
choices: 'on' | 'Click' | 'Focus'
'onClick' | 'onFocus'
`on${'click' | 'focus'}`
`on${string}`
questions.why: Template literal types distribute over unions and compose with the intrinsic string types (`Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize`). Handy for deriving prop names or route params from a string.
questions.asked: It shows whether you can read the type-level string tricks that libraries like routers use.

questions.q: Why is `error` typed `unknown` in this catch clause under `strict`?
questions.code: try { /* ... */ } catch (error) { }
choices: Because JavaScript can throw any value, not only `Error` objects
Because the compiler cannot see which function in the try block threw
Because `strict` forbids `any` anywhere, including in catch clauses
Because `Error` is a DOM type that is missing from the Node typings
questions.why: You can throw a string, a number, anything, so `strict` (via `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, TS 4.4+) types it `unknown`. Narrow with `error instanceof Error` before reading `.message`, and keep a fallback. Knowing which call threw would not help: the thrown value is still arbitrary.
questions.asked: It checks whether you write catch blocks that survive a thrown string.

questions.q: What is `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof loadUser>>` for?
choices: Marking `loadUser` as async so that its callers are forced to await it
Waiting for `loadUser` to finish at runtime before checking its type
Getting the resolved data type of an async function without exporting it
Converting a callback-style `loadUser` into a promise-returning version
questions.why: `ReturnType` gives `Promise<User>`, and `Awaited` unwraps promises recursively, leaving `User`. It is purely type-level; nothing runs. Useful when a function's result type is inferred and never named.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can derive types from existing code instead of duplicating them.

questions.q: `tsc` passes and the API responses are validated, yet the app crashes on bad data. Which boundary is most often forgotten?
choices: Values read back from `localStorage`, env vars or `postMessage`
Function arguments passed between two modules of the same app
Props passed from a parent component to a typed child component
Return values of functions that have explicit return annotations
questions.why: The compiler checks everything it can see, which includes calls between your own typed modules and components. Data from storage, the environment or another window arrives as strings or `any` and is unchecked until you check it; stale `localStorage` from an older release is the classic crash.
questions.asked: A scenario question that tests whether you know every place untyped data enters, not just HTTP.

questions.q: What is the difference between `Extract<T, U>` and `Exclude<T, U>`?
choices: Extract works on object keys; Exclude works on union members
They are identical apart from the order of their two arguments
Extract pulls out one property type; Exclude removes a property
Extract keeps union members assignable to U; Exclude drops them
questions.why: Both are conditional types that distribute over a union. `Exclude<Status, 'archived'>` derives a narrower state set from a wider one without duplicating the list. Removing object properties is `Omit`'s job.
questions.asked: It checks that you can derive types from one source of truth instead of copying unions.

questions.q: Which single tsconfig setting most improves type safety in a new project?
choices: `"noEmit": true`
`"strict": true`
`"target": "ES2022"`
`"allowJs": true`
questions.why: `strict` is an umbrella over `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes` and more. `noEmit` and `target` change output, not checking; `allowJs` lets unchecked files in. Add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` once the team is comfortable.
questions.asked: 'What's in your tsconfig?' is a quick way to gauge experience.

questions.q: What return type does TypeScript give `lineTotal`?
choices: `any`, because the return type was never annotated
`number`, inferred from what the function returns
`unknown`, until a return annotation is added
`number | undefined`, as `total` may be unset
questions.why: Return types are inferred from the `return` expressions, and `number * number` is `number`. Parameters are what need annotations. Many teams still annotate exported functions' return types so a body change cannot silently change the public contract.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know where annotations earn their keep and where inference already covers you.

questions.q: Under `strict`, why does `function greet(name) { return 'Hi ' + name; }` fail to compile?
choices: Under `strict` every function must declare its return type as well
Untyped parameters default to `unknown`, and `+` rejects `unknown`
Function declarations need a type parameter list when arguments are untyped
`name` has no type and nothing to infer one from, so it is implicitly `any`
questions.why: `noImplicitAny`, part of `strict`, rejects a parameter that would silently become `any`. Return types can still be inferred, and parameters do not default to `unknown`. The fix is `name: string`; callbacks passed inline usually get their parameter types from context instead.
questions.asked: The first error every JavaScript developer hits when a project turns on `strict`.

questions.q: What is the type of `count`?
questions.code:
const entry: [string, number] = ['apples', 3];
const [label, count] = entry;
choices: number
string | number
any
number | undefined
questions.why: A tuple type fixes the type at each position, so destructuring position 1 gives `number`. `string | number` is what you would get from a plain `(string | number)[]` array, which is what the literal infers without the annotation.
questions.asked: Tuples are how hooks like `useState` return pairs, so this checks you can read their types.

questions.q: What lets `p.number` compile on the last line?
choices: Reading a key on a union is allowed if at least one member has that key
`in` is a runtime check only, so the compiler stops checking later lines
The `in` check narrowed `p`, so after the early return only `Card` is left
The inferred return type is `string`, which forces both branches to agree
questions.why: `'iban' in p` narrows `p` to `Bank` inside the `if`, and the early return leaves only `Card` afterwards. Without narrowing, `p.number` would fail, because on a union you can only read keys every member has.
questions.asked: Narrowing on a key is how you handle unions that have no shared tag field, common with third-party payloads.

questions.q: Why does this fail under `strict`?
choices: `Object.keys` accepts only `Record<string, unknown>`, not `object`
`typeof x === 'object'` narrows to `object`, but `object` is not iterable
The two returns have different types, so the return type cannot be inferred
`typeof null` is `'object'`, so `x` is still `object | null` there
questions.why: The compiler models the JavaScript quirk: `typeof null === 'object'`, so the branch narrows to `object | null` and the `Object.keys(x)` call rejects the possible `null`. Check `x !== null` as well, or use `x && typeof x === 'object'`.
questions.asked: It links a classic JavaScript quirk to the compiler error it causes, which is what real debugging looks like.

questions.q: What is `User`?
choices: { name: string; createdAt: string }
(name: string) => { name: string }
{ name: string; createdAt: Date }
typeof makeUser
questions.why: `typeof makeUser` gives the function's type, and `ReturnType` extracts what it returns, so the object type is derived from the code instead of written twice. `createdAt` is `Date` here; it only becomes a string after a JSON round trip, which the type does not know about.
questions.asked: Deriving types from code keeps one source of truth, which reviewers value over hand-copied interfaces.

questions.q: With `type Person = { name: string; id: number }`, how do `const a: Person = { name: 'Al' }` and `const b = { name: 'Al' } as Person` differ?
choices: They both compile, and each object gets an `id` of `0` at runtime
`a` fails because `id` is missing; `b` compiles, since `as` checks far less
`a` compiles and `b` fails, because `as` requires every property to exist
`as` converts the object at runtime; the annotation checks at compile time
questions.why: An annotation checks the literal fully, so the missing `id` is an error. `as` only requires the types to overlap, so it accepts an incomplete object and `b.id` is `undefined` at runtime. Neither converts anything. Prefer annotations or `satisfies`.
questions.asked: Reviewers see `as` used to silence errors daily; this checks you know what it gives up.

questions.q: What is the type of `city`?
choices: string | undefined
string | null | undefined
string | null
{ city: string } | undefined
questions.why: Optional chaining short-circuits to `undefined` when `address` is missing, so the compiler adds `| undefined`. It never produces `null`, even when the value it stops at is `null`.
questions.asked: It checks that you read `?.` as changing the type, which explains the 'possibly undefined' errors that follow it.

questions.q: Why is `keys` typed `string[]` rather than `(keyof User)[]`?
choices: `Object.keys` is declared in the JavaScript lib without generics, so nothing can be inferred from `user`
It is `string[]` only because `User` is a type alias; an interface gives `(keyof User)[]` instead
`keyof User` is a union, and an array of a union is not a legal return type for a lib function
Structural typing lets `user` carry extra runtime keys, so `id` and `name` are not guaranteed to be all of them
questions.why: Any object with at least `id` and `name` is a `User`, so at runtime it may carry more keys than the type lists, and `(keyof User)[]` would be a lie. When you know the object is exactly a `User`, cast: `Object.keys(user) as (keyof User)[]`, or iterate a literal list of keys instead. Alias versus interface plays no part.
questions.asked: The 'string cannot be used to index type User' error that follows is one of the most googled TypeScript errors, and the reason is structural typing.
